abstract: Neural networks learn effective feature representations, which can be transferred to new tasks without additional training. While larger datasets are known to improve feature transfer, the theoretical conditions for the success of such transfer remain unclear. This work investigates feature transfer in networks trained for classification to identify the conditions that enable effective clustering in unseen classes. We first reveal that higher similarity between training and unseen distributions leads to improved Cohesion and Separability. We then show that feature expressiveness is enhanced when inputs are similar to the training classes, while the features of irrelevant inputs remain indistinguishable. We validate our analysis on synthetic and benchmark datasets, including CAR, CUB, SOP, ISC, and ImageNet. Our analysis highlights the importance of the similarity between training classes and the input distribution for successful feature transfer.

summary.idea: The paper analyzes feature transfer in a two-layer model, relating similarity to the training distribution to within-class cohesion and separation between classes.
summary.limitations: The theoretical model is simplified and asymptotic. The abstract does not provide a universal similarity measure or guarantee that the same quantitative relationship holds for every modern architecture and downstream task.
summary.problem: Features learned for classification are often reused to group previously unseen classes, but their success is not guaranteed. The relationship between training categories and new inputs may be crucial.
summary.results: The analysis predicts more expressive features for inputs resembling training classes and poorly distinguished features for irrelevant inputs. Synthetic and benchmark experiments support the role of distributional similarity in transfer quality.
summary.tldr: Transferred classification features work better when new inputs share relevant structure with the original training classes.

title: How Classifier Features Transfer to Downstream: An Asymptotic Analysis in a Two-Layer Model
